lead: A Gaussian process is a random process whose values at any finite set of times have a multivariate normal distribution. Its mean function and covariance function fix every such distribution, so these two functions describe the whole process. Gaussian noise uses the same idea for fluctuations: zero mean and a flat power spectral density. Engineers use it for thermal noise in receivers, for sensor errors, and for smoothing noisy data. The model is common because linear operations keep it Gaussian and because only first and second moments are needed.
prereq: You need: the multivariate normal from Unit 4, wide-sense stationarity from 7.2, and power spectral density from 7.7.

sections.h3: Definition and why mean and covariance suffice

blocks.text: A random process X(t) is Gaussian if, for every integer n ≥ 1 and every choice of times t₁,…,tₙ, the vector (X(t₁),…,X(tₙ)) has a multivariate normal distribution. Some syllabi call this a normal process. The finite-dimensional condition is the definition; having a normal marginal at each single time is not enough.
X(t) is Gaussian ⇔ (X(t₁),…,X(tₙ)) ~ N(μ, C) for every n and times t₁,…,tₙ
blocks.where: μ is the mean vector with entries μ(tᵢ)=E[X(tᵢ)]; C is the covariance matrix with entries C(tᵢ,tⱼ)=Cov(X(tᵢ),X(tⱼ)).

blocks.text: The mean function μ(t) gives the centre at each time. The covariance function C(s,t) gives the covariance between two times. For a Gaussian process these two functions determine every finite joint density, because a multivariate normal density is fixed by its mean vector and covariance matrix. No higher moments are needed.

If a Gaussian process is wide-sense stationary, μ(t)=μ is constant and C(s,t)=C(s−t)=C(τ). A time shift changes neither the constant mean nor any time difference, so every finite joint distribution is unchanged. Therefore a WSS Gaussian process is strictly stationary. This implication is special to Gaussian processes.

White Gaussian noise W(t) is a Gaussian process with zero mean and autocorrelation R_W(τ)=(N₀/2)δ(τ). Here N₀ is the one-sided noise power spectral density in watts per hertz, δ(τ) is the Dirac delta with unit 1/s, and the factor 1/2 comes from the two-sided convention. The corresponding two-sided power spectral density is flat: S_W(ω)=N₀/2 for all ω.

blocks.where: R_W(τ) is the autocorrelation at lag τ in watts; N₀ is the one-sided PSD in W/Hz; δ(τ) is the Dirac delta; S_W(ω) is the two-sided PSD in W/Hz.

blocks.text: Samples at distinct times are uncorrelated because R_W(τ)=0 for τ≠0. They are jointly Gaussian, so uncorrelated implies independent. Thus the ideal continuous-time model has independent samples at every distinct time.

The word white describes the flat spectrum. The word Gaussian describes the amplitude distribution. In the ideal model R_W(0) is infinite, so the variance is infinite; this is a mathematical idealisation. Real thermal noise is bandlimited and has finite power. A receiver's front end is often modelled as white Gaussian noise passed through a bandlimiting filter.

Pass a Gaussian process through a linear time-invariant (LTI) system. Every finite collection of output values is a linear combination of jointly Gaussian input values, so the output is also Gaussian. The mean and covariance change according to the system, but Gaussianity is preserved. This is why Gaussian models survive filtering, amplification and mixing.

For an LTI system with frequency response H(ω), the output mean is μ_Y=H(0)μ_X and the output power spectral density is S_Y(ω)=|H(ω)|²S_X(ω). These are the filtering rules from 7.8. For white Gaussian noise input, S_Y(ω)=|H(ω)|²N₀/2; the output is coloured Gaussian noise, not white unless |H(ω)| is constant.

Thermal noise in an antenna or resistor is modelled as white Gaussian noise over the receiver band. Receiver noise adds more such noise. The noise figure measures how much the receiver degrades the signal-to-noise ratio. A bandpass filter around a carrier gives narrowband Gaussian noise, common in radio receivers. In a simulation, you generate independent normal samples, then filter them.

examples.question: A Gaussian process X(t) has mean μ=2 and covariance C(τ)=9e^{−|τ|/2}, where τ is the time lag in seconds. (a) Find P(X(0)≤5). (b) Find Var[X(3)−X(0)]. Use Φ(1)=0.8413.
steps: At t=0, X(0) is normal with mean 2 and variance C(0)=9e⁰=9. Its standard deviation is √9 = 3.
For the difference, Var[X(3)−X(0)] = Var X(3)+Var X(0)−2Cov(X(3),X(0)).
examples.answer: P(X(0)≤5)=0.8413 and Var[X(3)−X(0)]≈13.98 in squared units of X.
examples.check:
import math
p = 0.5 * (1 + math.erf((5 - 2) / (3 * math.sqrt(2))))
v = 18 * (1 - math.exp(-1.5))
print(round(p, 4))
print(round(v, 2))

traps: Normal marginal distributions do not make a Gaussian process. Every finite joint distribution must be multivariate normal.
For a WSS Gaussian process, wide-sense stationarity implies strict stationarity. For a non-Gaussian WSS process, it does not.
The autocorrelation of ideal white noise is a Dirac delta, not a finite spike. R_W(0) is infinite in the ideal model.
N₀/2 is a two-sided PSD. The one-sided PSD is N₀; mixing the factor 2 halves or doubles the noise power.
Linear filtering changes the PSD and covariance of Gaussian noise but preserves Gaussianity. Do not assume the output is white.

quiz.a: For every n and every choice of times t₁,…,tₙ, the vector (X(t₁),…,X(tₙ)) has a multivariate normal distribution.

quiz.q: Why does wide-sense stationarity imply strict stationarity for a Gaussian process?
quiz.a: A finite joint normal distribution is fixed by its mean vector and covariance matrix. A time shift leaves the constant mean and all time differences unchanged, so no finite joint distribution changes.

quiz.q: A Gaussian process X(t) has mean 1 and covariance C(τ)=4e^{−|τ|}. Find P(X(0)≤3).
quiz.a: X(0) has mean 1 and variance 4, so standard deviation 2. P(X(0)≤3)=P(Z≤(3−1)/2)=Φ(1)=0.8413.

quiz.q: White Gaussian noise has two-sided PSD N₀/2=3×10⁻⁶ W/Hz. Write R_W(τ) and state the dependence between samples at distinct times.
quiz.a: R_W(τ)=3×10⁻⁶ δ(τ) W. Samples at distinct times are uncorrelated, and because they are jointly Gaussian they are independent.

quiz.q: A process has a normal marginal distribution at each time. Does that prove it is a Gaussian process? Explain.
quiz.a: No. A Gaussian process requires every finite collection to be jointly normal. Normal marginals do not determine the joint distribution.

quiz.q: White Gaussian noise passes through an LTI filter H(ω). Is the output Gaussian? Write its PSD.
quiz.a: Yes, a linear operation on jointly Gaussian values gives Gaussian output. The output PSD is S_Y(ω)=|H(ω)|²N₀/2.

quiz.q: A Gaussian process X(t) has mean 0 and covariance C(τ)=4e^{−|τ|}. Find Var[X(2)−X(0)].

beyond: Not for the exam. Gaussian process regression uses the same mean and covariance idea to fit smooth curves with uncertainty bands, and it appears in sensor fusion and Bayesian optimisation. In communications, AWGN models lead to link budgets and error-rate calculations. Search 'Gaussian process regression', 'Wiener filter' and 'noise figure'.
